note: Employers for the Draft Table. `sectors` are the career sectors it hires from (the first names it); it is only used where the place's careers include one. `roles` are the neighbourhoods it suits.

employers.summary: The castle household: stewards, grooms, cooks, guards and pages, the biggest employer in town by far.
The abbey, with its infirmary, school, guest hall and lands, hiring lay servants, scribes and nurses.
Smiths and armourers working for the castle, the farms and anyone with a horse that needs shoeing.
Weavers, fullers and dyers making the cloth the town is known for, sold at the fairs downriver.
The busiest inn in town, with brewers, cooks, tapsters and ostlers working all hours.
The bakers who bake the town's bread, and its pies on feast days.
Wool merchants trading fleeces and cloth to the coast, with clerks, packers and carters.
Watermen, ferrymen and bargees carrying goods and people up and down the water.
The mill grinding everyone's grain for a toll, with a miller, his boy and a waterman on the sluice.
The manor's fields, flocks and orchards outside the walls, busiest at harvest and lambing.
Masons, carpenters and labourers rebuilding the church tower, which they have been doing for forty years.
Woodcutters, charcoal burners and huntsmen working the forest under the eye of the verderer.
Musicians and players who perform at feasts, fairs and the inn yards, and want paying in advance.
Shoemakers, tailors and tanners, each a small shop with a master and two apprentices.
A hospital for the sick poor, with an infirmarer, nurses and an apothecary's garden.
The town's clerks, tollkeepers and watchmen, collecting dues and keeping the peace, mostly.
A great brick mill of spindles and looms, three hundred hands and a hooter at six.
Engine works building boilers, pumps and locomotives, the biggest employer in the valley.
The railway: drivers, porters, signalmen, clerks and the men in the sheds, all in company uniform.
Shipowners and the dock company, hiring dockers by the day and clerks by the year.
The bank on the square, its clerks in high collars and the manager who knows everyone's business.
The town newspaper, with reporters, compositors and a printing press that shakes the building at midnight.
The post office and telegraph, where messages from across the world arrive in minutes.
The big store on the high street, with shop assistants, floorwalkers and a delivery van.
The grand hotel, with waiters, chambermaids, cooks, a hall porter and a bar for the commercial gentlemen.
The infirmary, with doctors, nurses in starched caps and a matron who terrifies all of them.
The schools, with teachers, pupil-teachers and a headmaster who believes in the cane.
The servants' world of the big houses: maids, cooks, footmen and grooms, hired at the registry office.
Constables and detectives keeping order in the town, and the cells under the town hall.
Music hall and theatre folk: singers, actors, stagehands and the band.
The mine and stamp mill, running three shifts, hiring miners, millmen and an assayer.
Teamsters and stage drivers hauling freight and passengers to the railhead and the camps.
A big ranch running cattle over a hundred square miles, hiring cowhands for the roundup.
The army post outside town, troopers in blue, and a payday that keeps the saloons in business.
Smiths, laundresses and dressmakers, small shops working from dawn on whatever the town needs mended.
A foundry casting iron for engines and bridges, hot, loud and proud of its union.
Photographers and artists making portraits, postcards and the occasional scandal.
A factory of four floors making shoes, radios or corsets, depending on the decade's luck.
The bank in the skyscraper, tellers in cages and stockbrokers on the telephone to New York.
Six floors of department store with clerks, floorwalkers, window dressers and a lunch counter.
The daily paper and its radio station, reporters, linotype operators and announcers.
Rows of switchboard operators plugging in calls for the whole town, with supervisors walking behind.
Trawlers and the cannery by the wharf, busiest when the herring are running.
Longshoremen, motormen, conductors and dispatchers moving freight and people round the clock.
The railroad, from Pullman porters to freight clerks, with the station clock running everyone's day.
The big hotel and its dining room, with waiters, cooks, bellhops and a bartender who serves only soda, officially.
The clubs and theatres, with musicians, chorus girls, actors and stagehands working nights.
The general hospital, nurses in white, doctors with new X-ray machines and a druggist downstairs.
The college and the high school, with professors, teachers, librarians and a football coach.
Builders putting up bungalows and office blocks as fast as the banks will lend.
The police and the law firms, busy with Prohibition cases on both sides of the bench.
Chauffeurs, housemaids and cooks working in the big houses for families who never ask the price.
A granite quarry on the hill, blasting at noon, its stone in half the town's buildings.
The parish and the settlement house, running a school, a clinic, a soup kitchen and English classes.
The navy yard by the harbour, sailors on leave in town and a lot of work for the shipwrights.
The regional hospital: an emergency department, a cancer center and the biggest employer for fifty miles.
The college, with faculty, staff, grad students and a football team the town takes too seriously.
The school district: teachers, aides, counsellors, bus drivers and cafeteria staff.
A software company that outgrew a garage downtown and now has free snacks and a ping-pong table.
A regional bank and insurance office with analysts, accountants and a branch on every corner.
The big hotel by the convention center, front desk, housekeeping, banquets and a rooftop bar.
A local group running five restaurants and a bakery, always hiring cooks and servers.
The mall and its anchor store, with retail jobs that are always hiring before the holidays.
The local paper and its podcasts, with reporters, designers and a radio show on Sunday mornings.
A theater company and the design studio next door, actors, designers and a lot of freelancers.
City hall and county offices: planners, clerks, social workers and the people who fix the potholes.
The law firms round the courthouse, partners, paralegals and too many filing cabinets.
The port and distribution warehouses, forklifts, logistics coordinators and trucks at all hours.
A builder putting up apartments downtown and houses on the edge of town, hiring every trade.
Parks, pools and the rec center, with lifeguards, trainers and summer camp staff.
A biotech company in a glass building by the river, labs on every floor and a cafe for the scientists.
Tour boats, kayak rentals and guided walks for the summer visitors.
An estate agency on Main Street with photos of houses in the window and agents always on the phone.
A military base and the contractors round it, sailors, engineers and security clearances.
The engineers who keep the drive, the hull and the reactors running, on rotating watches.
Air, water and waste: the systems nobody notices until they fail, and the crews who make sure they don't.
The farms, orchards and aquaculture tanks that feed everyone, run by a council of growers.
The medical centre: doctors, nurses, medics and the counsellors who help people through the long voyage.
The academy and the archive, teaching every child aboard and keeping Earth's knowledge alive.
The council, its clerks and administrators, and the mediators who settle disputes before they fester.
Pilots, navigators and traffic controllers flying the ship and its shuttles.
Stores, cargo and rations: everything that goes in and out of the holds is counted here.
The galleys, mess halls and canteens, cooks and servers working round every shift.
Systems engineers, network crews and analysts keeping every screen, door and sensor talking.
Astronomers, biologists and materials scientists studying the stars ahead and the ship's own ecosystem.
Security, fire-and-pressure crews and rescue specialists, trained for emergencies that rarely come.
Shopkeepers, traders and repair stalls on the promenade, small businesses that make the place feel like a town.
Musicians, actors, designers and the immersive-room crews who keep everyone sane between ports.
Builders, welders and fitters adding new rings and refitting old cabins, and the electricians and plumbers who follow.
Asteroid surveyors and ore-processing engineers, working the rocks the ship passes.
Fabricators and machinists making every spare part aboard, because there is nowhere to order one from.
Carpenters and wheelwrights building carts, roofs and coffins, and arguing about the price of oak.
Fishing boats and the harbour reeve's men, out with the tide and selling the catch on the stones.
Dyers and tanners working the vats and pits downstream, well paid for the smell.
The great house of the bishop or the lord of the manor, with cooks, maids, grooms and a steward who counts the candles.
Garages, radio repair and the new electrical trades, mechanics in coveralls and a boy to pump gas.
The amusement park and country club, lifeguards, caddies, ride operators and a summer dance band.
The fishing fleet, the boatyard and the fish market, early mornings and a smell you get used to.
Orchards and a farm stand on the edge of town, pick-your-own in the fall and a bakery that sells the pies.
Gene therapists and lab technicians keeping the population healthy and the crops resilient.
The ship's news feed and broadcasts: reporters, broadcasters and the person who reads out the birthdays.
Fitness coaches, pool attendants and zero-g coaches running the required exercise hours and the leagues.
Accountants, brokers and assessors keeping track of credits, claims and trade.
